blocks.content: 1. INTRODUCTION TO CONJUNCTIONS

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Coordinating conjunctions are categorized using the FANBOYS acronym.
Double conjunction usage is one of the most common error types tested in SSC exams.
Correlative conjunctions require strict adherence to parallel structure and subject-verb agreement rules.
Pairs such as 'No sooner... than' and 'Hardly... when' trigger obligatory inversion rules.
Words like 'Unless' and 'Until' carry negative meaning inherently and differ fundamentally in time versus action logic.

blocks.content:
A conjunction is a word that joins words, phrases, clauses, or sentences and establishes a logical relationship between them.



Conjunction-based questions are VERY frequent in SSC exams because they test logic, grammar, and sentence structure simultaneously.



Golden Principle:

The conjunction you choose must reflect the logical relationship — not just grammatical correctness.
2. COMPLETE CLASSIFICATION OF CONJUNCTIONS

There are three primary categories:



1. Coordinating Conjunctions – Join equal clauses.

2. Subordinating Conjunctions – Join dependent clauses to independent clauses.

3. Correlative Conjunctions – Work in pairs.



Additionally, SSC frequently tests:

• Conjunction vs Preposition confusion

• Conditional conjunctions

• Contrast conjunctions

• Result conjunctions

• Time conjunctions
3. COORDINATING CONJUNCTIONS (FANBOYS)

FANBOYS:



For – reason

And – addition

Nor – negative addition

But – contrast

Or – choice

Yet – unexpected contrast

So – result



IMPORTANT SSC RULE:

Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction when joining two independent clauses.



Example:

He was tired, but he continued working.
4. MOST COMMON SSC ERROR – DOUBLE CONJUNCTION

Never use two conjunctions for the same purpose.



Incorrect:

Although he was tired but he worked hard.



Correct:

Although he was tired, he worked hard.

OR

He was tired, but he worked hard.



Other Examples:



Incorrect: Because it was raining so we stayed home.

Correct: Because it was raining, we stayed home.
5. SUBORDINATING CONJUNCTIONS – LOGIC BASED USAGE

Subordinating conjunctions introduce dependent clauses.



CAUSE:

because, since, as



CONTRAST:

although, though, even though, whereas



CONDITION:

if, unless, provided that, in case



TIME:

when, while, before, after, until, as soon as



RESULT:

so that, such that
6. BECAUSE vs SINCE vs AS (VERY IMPORTANT)

Because → Strong, direct reason.

Since → Reason already known.

As → Used when reason is less important.



SSC Tip:

Prefer "because" in formal grammar questions when the reason is the focus.
7. ALTHOUGH / THOUGH / EVEN THOUGH

All show contrast, but intensity differs.



Though → mild contrast

Although → stronger

Even though → strongest



RULE:

Never use 'but' with these.
8. UNLESS – ONE OF THE MOST TESTED CONJUNCTIONS

Unless means "if not".



Incorrect:

Unless you do not study, you will fail.



Correct:

Unless you study, you will fail.



IMPORTANT:

Do not add another negative word.
9. UNTIL vs UNLESS

Until → refers to time.

Unless → refers to condition.



Example:

Wait until I return.

You cannot enter unless you have permission.
10. LEST – ADVANCED SSC FAVORITE

Lest means "so that not".



RULE:

Always use 'should' after lest.



Example:

Work hard lest you should fail.



Never use 'not' after lest.
11. CORRELATIVE CONJUNCTIONS – FULL RULE SET

Common pairs:



either…or

neither…nor

both…and

not only…but also

whether…or

no sooner…than

hardly…when

scarcely…when
12. SUBJECT–VERB AGREEMENT WITH CORRELATIVES

With either…or / neither…nor → verb agrees with nearest subject.



Example:

Either the teacher or the students are responsible.

Either the students or the teacher is responsible.
13. NOT ONLY…BUT ALSO – PARALLELISM RULE

Both elements must be grammatically similar.



Incorrect:

She is not only intelligent but also has discipline.



Correct:

She is not only intelligent but also disciplined.
14. NO SOONER…THAN / HARDLY…WHEN (INVERSION RULE)

rows: 'Until' is time-oriented (up to the point in time), whereas 'Unless' is condition-oriented (if not).
No sooner... than vs Hardly... when
'No sooner' strictly pairs with 'than'; 'Hardly' or 'Scarcely' strictly pairs with 'when' or 'before'.
'So... that' modifies adjectives/adverbs, while 'Such... that' modifies noun phrases.
'Whether' is used when offering choices/alternatives (often with 'or'); 'If' introduces conditional clauses.

blocks.content:
These require inversion.



Structure:

No sooner + had + subject + V3 + than…



Example:

No sooner had he arrived than it started raining.
15. WHETHER vs IF

Use WHETHER when alternatives exist.



Example:

I don’t know whether he will come or not.



Use IF for conditions.
16. SO…THAT vs SUCH…THAT

SO + adjective/adverb

SUCH + noun



Example:

It was so hot that we stayed inside.

It was such a hot day that we stayed inside.
17. AS SOON AS – FUTURE TRAP

Do NOT use future tense in the clause.



Incorrect:

As soon as he will arrive…



Correct:

As soon as he arrives…
18. PROVIDED THAT / IN CASE / EVEN IF

Provided that → condition

In case → precaution

Even if → hypothetical condition



SSC frequently tests these subtle differences.
19. CONJUNCTION vs PREPOSITION (VERY HIGH SSC TRAP)

After a preposition → noun/gerund.

After a conjunction → clause.



Example:

He succeeded because of hard work. (preposition)

He succeeded because he worked hard. (conjunction)
20. COMMONLY CONFUSED PAIRS

While vs Whereas

So vs Therefore

Till vs By the time

Before vs Ago



Understanding the logical difference is crucial.

items: Always pair 'No sooner' with 'than' (not 'when') and 'Hardly/Scarcely' with 'when' (not 'than'), ensuring auxiliary verb inversion.
Never use negative words like 'not' or 'no' in clauses introduced by 'Unless', 'Until', or 'Lest'.
Do not combine redundant conjunctions together in the same sentence (Double Conjunction error).

blocks.content: 21. HIGH-PROBABILITY SSC RULES

1. Avoid double conjunctions.

2. Maintain parallel structure.

3. Learn correlative pairs.

4. Use inversion correctly.

5. Do not use future after time conjunctions.

6. Match conjunction with logic.
22. COMMON ERRORS IN SSC EXAMS

Incorrect: Neither he nor his friends was present.

Correct: Neither he nor his friends were present.



Incorrect: No sooner he arrived than it rained.

Correct: No sooner had he arrived than it rained.



Incorrect: She is both smart as well as hardworking.

Correct: She is both smart and hardworking.
23. PRACTICE QUESTIONS (SSC LEVEL)

Fill in the blanks:



1. Work fast ___ you will miss the train.

2. No sooner had she entered ___ everyone stood up.

3. Neither the manager nor the employees ___ willing.



Error Detection:



1. Although he was ill but he attended.

2. Unless you do not hurry, you will be late.

3. Hardly I had reached when it started raining.



Answers:

or, than, were



Errors:

remove 'but'

remove double negative

use inversion
24. CHAPTER SUMMARY

Conjunctions are the backbone of logical sentence construction.



Key Takeaways:



• Choose conjunctions based on logic.

• Avoid double conjunction errors.

• Master correlative pairs.

• Learn inversion structures.

• Practice contrast and condition connectors.
